claims.text: FeNiCrMn HEA has excellent corrosion resistance.
The local-scale mechanical properties of as-processed FeNiCrMn HEA are uncharacterized.
Instrumented nanoindentation coupled with micro-pillar compression or in situ SEM tensile testing can resolve local mechanical responses in distinct microstructural regions.
As-processed FeNiCrMn HEA will exhibit marked spatial variations in hardness, elastic modulus, and yielding behavior.
The predicted spatial variations in mechanical behavior arise from intrinsic microstructural heterogeneity.
Moderately elevated test temperatures are representative of aerospace, energy, and automotive service conditions.
Grain boundaries, dislocation networks, and phase distributions may produce stress concentrations and variable deformation responses in FeNiCrMn HEA.
Intrinsic microstructural heterogeneity causes spatial variations in dislocation activity and plastic deformation.
Spatial variations in dislocation activity and plastic deformation cause local differences in hardness and elastic modulus.
Conventional bulk tests cannot detect the proposed local differences in hardness and elastic modulus.
Local measurements will show statistically significant regional differences in hardness, elastic modulus, and yield behavior.
Spatially resolved measurements will provide insight into local deformation mechanisms that are averaged out by bulk mechanical tests.
Conventional tensile and compression tests provide average mechanical-property values and do not resolve specific local microstructural effects.
The hypothesis is restricted to as-processed FeNiCrMn HEA under laboratory-scale testing.
Results may not extend to extensively thermomechanically processed alloys or extreme service conditions.
The magnitude of the spatial variations and the relative contributions of individual microstructural features are unknown.
In situ SEM tensile testing can directly observe dislocation dynamics and deformation mechanisms in the proposed specimens.
A lack of statistically significant regional variations in hardness, modulus, and yield parameters would falsify the hypothesis.
